137-r1.sourceTitle: Euler Calculus with Applications to Signals and Sensing
137-r1.locator: Section 7, Lemma 7.1 and its proof, p. 11
137-r1.proofSketch: Over a chain complex of vector spaces, write $Z_k=\ker\partial_k$ and $B_k=\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$. Since $H_k=Z_k/B_k$ one has $\dim Z_k=\dim H_k+\dim B_k$. Because $\partial^2=0$, $C_k/Z_k\cong B_{k-1}$, so $\dim C_k=\dim Z_k+\dim B_{k-1}$. Combining, $\dim C_k=\dim H_k+\dim B_k+\dim B_{k-1}$. Multiply by $(-1)^k$ and sum over $k$; the boundary terms telescope, leaving $\sum(-1)^k\dim C_k=\sum(-1)^k\dim H_k$.

137-r1.attribution: Robert Ghrist, Euler calculus with applications to signals and sensing (arXiv:1202.0275)

137-r2.sourceTitle: Euler Calculus with Applications to Signals and Sensing
137-r2.locator: Section 7, Lemma 7.1 and its proof, p. 11
137-r2.proofSketch: Over a field, set $Z_k=\ker\partial_k$, $B_k=\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}\subseteq Z_k$, $H_k=Z_k/B_k$. Splitting $Z_k=B_k\oplus H_k'$ and $C_k=Z_k\oplus D_k$ with $D_k\cong B_{k-1}$ via $\partial_k$ gives $\dim C_k=\dim B_k+\dim H_k+\dim B_{k-1}$; the alternating sum then telescopes to the homology dimensions. The cited source argues with quotients and dimension counts rather than explicit complements.

images.caption: Ghrist, arXiv:1202.0275, p. 11: Lemma 7.1 and proof (dimension-count version of the same decomposition)

137-r2.attribution: Robert Ghrist, Euler calculus with applications to signals and sensing (arXiv:1202.0275)
137-r2.transcriptionNotes: The source never writes explicit complement subspaces; it uses $\dim Z_k=\dim H_k+\dim B_k$ and $C_k/Z_k\cong B_{k-1}$, which is the same decomposition at the level of dimensions.
137-r2.reasonNotReproduced: No openly accessible source found that writes the explicit direct-sum splitting into boundaries, homology representatives and complements; the nearest proof is the dimension-count argument shown.

137-r3.proofSketch: For a chain complex of finitely generated abelian groups with cycles $Z_n$, boundaries $B_n$ and homology $H_n=Z_n/B_n$ there are short exact sequences $0\to Z_n\to C_n\to B_{n-1}\to 0$ and $0\to B_n\to Z_n\to H_n\to 0$. Additivity of rank on short exact sequences gives $\operatorname{rank}C_n=\operatorname{rank}Z_n+\operatorname{rank}B_{n-1}$ and $\operatorname{rank}Z_n=\operatorname{rank}B_n+\operatorname{rank}H_n$. Substitute, multiply by $(-1)^n$ and sum: boundary ranks cancel, giving $\sum(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}C_n=\sum(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}H_n$. Applied to cellular chains this gives $\chi(X)=\sum(-1)^n\operatorname{rank}H_n(X)$.

142-r1.proofSketch: Let $G$ be a finite subgroup of $F^\times$. In a finite abelian group, elements of orders $n_1,n_2$ yield an element of order $\operatorname{lcm}(n_1,n_2)$. Hence if $n$ is the maximal element order, every element order divides $n$. So every element of $G$ is a root of $X^n-1$, giving $\#G\le n$ since a polynomial has at most $\deg$ roots in a field. Also $n$ divides $\#G$ by Lagrange, so $n=\#G$ and some element has order $\#G$, i.e. $G$ is cyclic.

images.caption: Conrad, Cyclotomic Extensions, p. 1: Theorem 1.1 and proof

142-r2.sourceTitle: Finite Multiplicative Subgroups of a Field
142-r2.proofSketch: All proofs rest on the fact that $x^d=1$ has at most $d$ solutions in a field. Using the structure theorem for finite abelian groups: if $|G|=n$ and $G$ is not cyclic, the invariant-factor decomposition gives a $d<n$ (the exponent) with $x^d=1$ for all $x\in G$. That gives more than $d$ roots of $x^d-1$, a contradiction, so $G$ is cyclic.
142-r2.attribution: Keith Conrad, Finite Multiplicative Subgroups of a Field (Stanford Math 210B handout)
142-r2.transcriptionNotes: Proof (I) is two sentences; the handout's Proofs (II) and (III) are omitted.

142-r3.sourceTitle: Finite Multiplicative Subgroups of a Field
142-r3.proofSketch: Apply the structure theorem to the finite abelian group $G\subset F^\times$: if $G$ is not cyclic there is $d<|G|$ with $x^d=1$ for all $x\in G$, impossible because $X^d-1$ has at most $d$ roots in a field. For $\mu_n$ in a field, the same argument shows the roots of unity form a cyclic group.
142-r3.attribution: Keith Conrad, Finite Multiplicative Subgroups of a Field (Stanford Math 210B handout)
142-r3.transcriptionNotes: Same proof as 142-r2; the handout treats general finite subgroups of $F^\times$ (which includes roots of unity) and does not separately discuss roots of unity.
142-r3.reasonNotReproduced: Route differs from 142-r2 only in framing (roots of unity); no separate source found.
